en: The national flower, Sampaguita, releases its strongest fragrance at night to attract nocturnal moth pollinators.
The national tree, Narra, drops its leaves during the dry season to conserve water before blooming yellow flowers.
The national bird, the Philippine eagle, hunts flying lemurs in the forest canopy using its exceptional binocular vision.
The Ifugao built the Banaue Rice Terraces using stone walls that prevent soil erosion and naturally filter irrigation water.
The Philippine tarsier has enormous eyes fixed in its skull, requiring it to rotate its head 180 degrees to see.
The national animal, the carabao, wallows in mud because it lacks sweat glands and uses mud to cool down.
The Queen of Philippine Orchids, Vanda sanderiana, uses aerial roots to absorb moisture directly from the humid forest air.
Marine biologist Angel Alcala proved that coral reefs recover faster when local communities protect them from destructive fishing.
The Lucban Pahiyas Festival decorates homes with kiping, which are leaf-shaped wafers made from ground rice and natural plant dyes.
Farmers wrap Philippine Carabao mangoes in paper to trap ethylene gas, a natural plant hormone that accelerates fruit ripening.
Abaca, a native banana plant, yields the world's strongest natural leaf fiber because of its exceptionally long cellulose strands.
Synchronized fireflies produce cold blue-green light through a chemical reaction between luciferin and oxygen inside their abdomens.
